title: On the Wire: Where a Control's Truth Travels
primary_engine: visual (PEEL primary; TRACE + MAP secondary); Diff-the-Trace for assessment
objectives: Explain, to a non-technical colleague, encapsulation as nesting — one captured frame is literally Ethernet{IPv4{TCP{TLS{HTTP}}}}, and frame/packet/segment name the same bytes at different layers — mapping each real header to its OSI layer (Ethernet=L2, IPv4=L3, TCP/UDP=L4, TLS~=L6, HTTP=L7) with the honest caveat that the wire runs TCP/IP and OSI is the teaching scaffold.

Locate where a given control claim's truth physically lives on the wire: which layer, header, and byte-offset holds it — MAC=hop-truth (L2), IP=end-to-end-truth (L3), port=service-exposure-truth (L4), TLS ContentType=in-transit-encryption-truth (L6), HTTP start-line=application-intent-truth (L7).

Query a real packet by reading the actual bytes — decode EtherType, IPv4 Protocol, src/dst IP, TCP src/dst port and flag bits, TLS ContentType from their RFC-fixed offsets — and answer a control question directly from the field values.
Describe the TCP 3-way handshake as a real state transition readable in the flag bits, and contrast TCP vs UDP and MAC-vs-IP addressing scope by reading the same packet at two hops.

Compose the 5-tuple (src IP, dst IP, protocol, src port, dst port) from a peeled packet and express the three most-audited network controls as predicates over those fields — segmentation (SC-7), encryption-in-transit (SC-8), port-exposure (CM-7).
Diagnose, in a forensic Diff-the-Trace of two real captures, the single field/byte where evidence contradicts a control claim, and name the control it breaks and the framework reference.
visual_for_abstractions: Encapsulation, layering, and addressing-scope become literal DOM regions. PEEL renders one real captured frame as nested expandable byte-range regions Ethernet{IPv4{TCP{TLS{HTTP}}}}. The clarifying abstraction (MAC=hop-truth changes per hop, IP=end-to-end-truth preserved) is shown by PEELing the SAME logical packet at two routers side by side: L2 MAC regions visibly differ, L3 IP regions visibly identical. The TCP handshake's connection-state-in-the-flag-bits is shown by selecting offset 13 and watching the 8-bit flags field decode to SYN/SYN+ACK/ACK across three real packets. Protocol-selection (Protocol=6 choosing the TCP parser) is shown as the PEEL tree refusing to expand an L4 region until the learner reads the selector byte.

activities.name: PEEL the Google search — one frame, five nested layers
activities.mechanic: The exemplar. The learner loads ONE real captured frame from the google.com search journey and works down the encapsulation stack as nested keyboard-selectable DOM byte-range regions: Ethernet{IPv4{TCP{TLS{HTTP}}}}. Each region stays collapsed until the learner reads the selector byte that justifies expanding the next layer — selecting Ethernet's EtherType (offset 12-13) reveals 0x0800 and unlocks IPv4; IPv4's Protocol byte (offset 9) reveals 0x06 and unlocks TCP. For each layer the prompt is 'which OSI layer is this, and what control-truth does it carry?'
activities.sim_state: A real frame from a downloaded google-search pcap (or stitched from Wireshark SampleCaptures: TLS leg from a real TLS 1.3 capture, cleartext-contrast leg from http.cap). The TS dissector (ported from RFC 791/9293/768/8446 byte layouts + IANA EtherType/Protocol registries) parses the actual bytes into the PEEL tree; the byte buffer and parse tree are the seeded state.

tasks.instruction: Select the EtherType region (2 bytes at offset 12-13). Label this region with its OSI layer, then state what value tells the dissector the payload is IPv4.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (selected range == dissector's Ethernet/EtherType range 12-13, label 'L2'); field_value_is (entered EtherType == 0x0800).
hint_ladder: The frame begins with two MAC addresses (6 bytes each); the 2-byte type tag follows.
§ Encapsulation — EtherType > 0x0600 marks Ethernet II and names the L3 payload.
Offset 12-13 reads 0x0800 = IPv4 (L3); label the Ethernet header L2.

tasks.instruction: Descend into IPv4. Select the Protocol field (byte at IPv4 offset 9), label the IPv4 region, and state which L4 parser this byte selects.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (offset 9, label 'L3'); field_value_is (0x06 = 6 = TCP per IANA Protocol Numbers).
hint_ladder: RFC 791 fixes the IPv4 header; the L4 selector is one byte, nine in.
§ Protocol field — 6=TCP, 17=UDP, 1=ICMP.
Offset 9 reads 0x06 -> TCP; label IPv4 as L3.

tasks.instruction: Descend to the TLS record and select the ContentType byte (first byte of the record). Label its OSI layer and state, from the value alone, whether the payload is encrypted or cleartext.
tasks.machine_verify: field_value_is (0x17 / 23 = application_data on the encrypted leg per RFC 8446); region_labeled_correctly (TLS ContentType byte, label 'L6').
hint_ladder: RFC 8446 puts ContentType as the very first byte of every TLS record.
§ Encryption in transit — 22=handshake (cleartext), 23=application_data (encrypted).
0x17 (23) = application_data: opaque/encrypted. Label TLS as ~L6.

activities.honesty_source: Every shown value is the TS dissector's output over real captured bytes (Wireshark SampleCaptures + a real TLS 1.3 capture). Field meanings: RFC 791, RFC 8446, IANA EtherType + Protocol Numbers. The dissector is fidelity-checked against tshark's decode of the same file; the parse tree IS the oracle.
activities.new_engine_work: The new `visual` Lab Player surface (Inspect-&-Assemble) with PEEL mode: DOM byte-range regions with ARIA, keyboard selection, and a TS port of the Ethernet/IPv4/TCP/TLS dissector. New verifier primitives region_labeled_correctly and field_value_is.

activities.name: MAC is hop-truth, IP is end-to-end — peel the same packet at two routers
activities.mechanic: Side-by-side PEEL of the SAME logical packet captured at two points (before-router-1, after-router-1). The learner selects L2 src/dst MAC regions in both and observes they DIFFER; selects L3 src/dst IP regions in both and observes they are IDENTICAL. Then answers a control question: 'an internal log shows source MAC X — can you attribute the originating host by it across a routed boundary?' (no — MAC is hop-local) vs the IP (end-to-end, attributable).
activities.sim_state: Two real captures of the same flow at adjacent hops, each parsed by the dissector. Two byte buffers + two parse trees aligned on the same L3 identification field so the learner can confirm it is the same packet.

tasks.instruction: Select the destination MAC region (L2) in BOTH captures and report same/different. Label what scope a MAC address has.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (both selections == each capture's L2 dst-MAC range); field_value_is (verdict == dissector's byte-comparison: different).
hint_ladder: Both frames start with dst MAC then src MAC; compare the first 6 bytes.
§ Addressing at two scopes — L2 MAC is hop-to-hop, rewritten at every router.
The two dst MACs differ: the router rewrote L2. MAC scope = hop-local.

tasks.instruction: Select the source IP region (L3, IPv4 offset 12-15) in BOTH and report same/different; label IP scope and which one attributes the host across the routed boundary.
tasks.machine_verify: field_value_is (verdict == comparison of the two L3 src-IP ranges: same); region_labeled_correctly (IPv4 src-address 12-15, label 'L3').
hint_ladder: The IPv4 source address sits at offset 12-15.
§ MAC vs IP — the IP is end-to-end, preserved across hops.
Both src IPs identical: IP scope = end-to-end. Attribute by IP, not MAC.

activities.honesty_source: Both captures are real packets parsed by the same fidelity-checked dissector; the same/different verdicts are byte comparisons the dissector computes. RFC 791 fixes the IP-address offsets.
activities.new_engine_work: Reuses PEEL surface + dissector; adds a two-pane aligned-capture layout. No new primitive.

activities.name: Assemble the TCP 3-way handshake — connection state in the flag bits
activities.mechanic: Participant nodes (client, server) + three real packet-cards from the capture's handshake, each carrying its real seq/ack and flags byte (offset 13). The learner orders cards: SYN(client->server, 0x02) -> SYN+ACK(server->client, 0x12) -> ACK(client->server, 0x10). A stateful counterpart enforces the RFC 9293 state machine: drop the ACK or reorder and the sim answers with a real RST / refuses ESTABLISHED — an honest consequence.
activities.sim_state: Three real handshake packets extracted from the google-search pcap (real seq/ack/flags). The TRACE counterpart follows the RFC 9293 state machine; seeded state is the three cards + the sim's CLOSED/LISTEN start.

tasks.instruction: Order the three handshake cards between client and server so the connection reaches ESTABLISHED. The server rejects an out-of-order message with the real consequence.
tasks.machine_verify: sequence_matches (ordered cards == RFC 9293 SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK with correct routing; sim reaches ESTABLISHED, emits RST on wrong order).
hint_ladder: The client proposes, the server agrees-and-proposes, the client confirms — three messages.
§ TCP 3-way handshake — SYN(seq=X) -> SYN+ACK(seq=Y,ack=X+1) -> ACK(ack=Y+1).
Client SYN, server SYN+ACK, client ACK; the ack numbers prove the order.

tasks.instruction: Select the flags byte (offset 13) on each card and read its bits. State which flag(s) are set on each and what state each represents.
tasks.machine_verify: field_value_is (decode per card == dissector decode: 0x02=SYN, 0x12=SYN+ACK, 0x10=ACK per bit order CWR,ECE,URG,ACK,PSH,RST,SYN,FIN).
hint_ladder: The 8 control flags share one byte at offset 13.
§ Flags ARE the state — SYN opens, SYN+ACK accepts, ACK confirms.
Card1=0x02 (SYN), card2=0x12 (SYN+ACK), card3=0x10 (ACK).

activities.honesty_source: Packet-cards carry real seq/ack/flags from the capture; flag decodes are the dissector's output; the TRACE counterpart runs the real RFC 9293 state machine, so a wrong order produces a real RST.
activities.new_engine_work: TRACE mode: participant nodes, orderable packet-cards (roving-tabindex listbox), a stateful TCP counterpart (RFC 9293 open). New primitive sequence_matches; reuses field_value_is.

activities.name: The 5-tuple is the firewall rule — map controls onto the fields you peeled
activities.mechanic: The bridge from QUERY to EVIDENCE/MONITOR. The peeled fields of a real packet (src IP, dst IP, IPv4 Protocol, TCP src/dst port) are draggable item-cards placed into a 5-tuple firewall-ACL structure. Then three control claims map onto their predicate: 'only 443 exposed' -> dst-port==443 (CM-7/SC-7); 'encrypted in transit' -> reads TLS ContentType not the 5-tuple (SC-8) — a deliberate trap; 'prod subnet segmented' -> src/dst IP range (SC-7). A second board places each claim onto its NIST 800-53 / SOC 2 zone, key cited.
activities.sim_state: The real peeled field values from the PEEL exemplar become the draggable cards. The zone key is derived from NIST 800-53 Rev.5 SC-7/SC-8/CM-7 and SOC 2 CC6.6/CC6.7, cited.

tasks.instruction: Drag each of the five peeled fields into its slot in the 5-tuple firewall-ACL structure.
tasks.machine_verify: mapping_correct (every field-card in the slot the closed key assigns; partial-credit gap names any misplaced field).
hint_ladder: A packet filter decides on five things: from, to, protocol, two ports.
§ Firewalls as field-readers — 5-tuple = L3 src/dst IP + L4 protocol + src/dst port.
src/dst IP from L3, protocol from offset 9, src/dst port from TCP offset 0-3.

tasks.instruction: Map each of the three control-claim cards onto the field/layer that decides it and onto its NIST 800-53 control zone. One claim does NOT live in the 5-tuple — find it.
tasks.machine_verify: mapping_correct (port-exposure->CM-7/SC-7 dst-port; segmentation->SC-7 IP-range; encryption-in-transit->SC-8, decided by TLS ContentType at L6, NOT the 5-tuple).
hint_ladder: Two claims are predicates over the 5-tuple; one is a byte at a different layer.
§ Three control families on the wire — SC-7, CM-7, SC-8.
'Encrypted in transit' is the odd one out — TLS ContentType (L6 / SC-8), not port or IP.

activities.honesty_source: Draggable field values are the real peeled bytes from the PEEL exemplar. The zone key cites NIST 800-53 Rev.5 SC-7/SC-8/CM-7 and SOC 2 TSC CC6.6/CC6.7 — an authoritative cited key.
activities.new_engine_work: MAP mode (drag/keyboard-assign to zones, ARIA aria-grabbed/aria-dropeffect). New primitive mapping_correct (every item in its authoritative zone, partial-credit gap). region_labeled_correctly + field_value_is share schema { check, region:{start,end}|value, expect, from?:generated } validated against the dissector's parse tree.

activities.name: Diff-the-Trace — find the one byte that breaks the claim (assessment)
activities.mechanic: The EVALUATE-stage forensic assessment. Three pairs of real captures (one clean, one carrying a real control failure) as side-by-side PEEL trees. For each pair the learner clicks the single differing byte-range that breaks the stated control claim, then writes a 'Wire Evidence Finding' naming the field, both values, the broken control, and the framework ref. Pair A: dst-port 0x0050 (80) vs clean 0x01BB (443) — CM-7/SC-7. Pair B: a cleartext HTTP start-line (real http.cap GET) vs clean ContentType 0x17 application_data — SC-8/CC6.7. Pair C: a real unsolicited ARP reply (opcode 2, no matching request) rebinding the gateway vs a clean request/reply — SC-7 trust assumption.
activities.sim_state: Three pairs of real pcaps: clean legs from Wireshark SampleCaptures (http.cap, dns.cap) + a real TLS 1.3 capture; failure legs are real instances (genuine port-80 exchange, genuine cleartext http.cap, genuine gratuitous-ARP capture). All parsed by the same dissector; the differing byte is the dissector's computed diff.

tasks.instruction: For each of the three pairs, click the single byte-range where the bad capture contradicts its stated control claim.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (per pair the selected range == dissector's computed discriminating diff: TCP dst-port for A, TLS ContentType / HTTP start-line offset for B, ARP opcode+sender-binding for C).
hint_ladder: Both captures are real and nearly identical — exactly one field carries the violation.
§ A control is a predicate over bytes — exposure->L4 port, encryption->L6 ContentType, L2 trust->ARP.
A: dst port 0x0050(80) not 0x01BB(443). B: cleartext GET where ContentType should be 0x17. C: ARP opcode 2 with no request.

tasks.instruction: Write one Wire Evidence Finding per pair: field, clean value, bad value, control claim broken, framework ref (SC-7, SC-8, or CM-7).
tasks.machine_verify: file_content_matches (each finding names the correct field token, byte/port/opcode values, matching framework regex); file_not_matches guards against citing the wrong control family.
hint_ladder: State it like an auditor: claim, field, expected, observed, control id.
§ The auditor frame — the owner CLAIMS, the wire is ground truth.
Pair A -> CM-7/SC-7. Pair B -> SC-8. Pair C -> SC-7.

activities.honesty_source: Both captures in every pair are real pcap bytes; failure legs are real instances of the misconfiguration; the discriminating byte is the dissector's diff over real bytes. Framework refs: NIST 800-53 Rev.5 SC-7/SC-8/CM-7, SOC 2 TSC CC6.6/CC6.7.
activities.new_engine_work: Diff-the-Trace layout (two aligned PEEL panes + per-diff click target). Reuses region_labeled_correctly, file_content_matches, file_not_matches — no new primitive.

assessment: Forensic Diff-the-Trace competency artifact. THREE pairs of real captures (one clean, one carrying a real control failure); unaided, the learner PEELs to the exact differing byte-range and produces a written Wire Evidence Finding per pair (field, two values, control claim broken, framework ref). region_labeled_correctly gates the exact discriminating byte; file_content_matches gates the written finding. Honesty: both captures in every pair are real pcap bytes and the 'differing byte' is the dissector's computed diff.

title: From a URL in a Box to a Chain of Trust: Reading the Request Lifecycle on the Wire
primary_engine: visual (PEEL | TRACE) with a Diff-the-Trace assessment
objectives: Explain, to a non-technical colleague, how typing google.com becomes one continuous chain of trust — a name resolved (DNS), a transport opened (TCP), a channel secured (TLS), a conversation held (HTTP), pixels rendered — and why each hop is a place a control claim can be made or broken.
Describe recursive vs iterative resolution and map the DNS treasure hunt root->TLD->authoritative onto where control-truth physically lives (NS delegation, CAA, SPF/DKIM/DMARC).
Map raw DNS message bytes to their RFC 1035 structural regions (header flags-word, QNAME labels, RR TYPE/CLASS/TTL/RDATA) and read the encoded values directly off the wire.
Locate the encryption boundary in the request lifecycle precisely — DNS, the TCP handshake, and the TLS SNI as plaintext-by-default, and TLS-on-443 as where confidentiality begins.
Compose the full type-to-render protocol sequence in correct order across DNS/TCP/TLS/HTTP, including the TCP ack=seq+1 invariant and the post-ServerHello encryption point.

Diagnose a broken control by reading it off real evidence — CAA absent, DMARC p=none, plaintext HTTP on 80, expired/wrong-host cert, or an unvalidated (AD-clear) DNS answer — and tie each to its control family (SC-8/SC-12/SC-17/SC-23, SI-8, SOC 2 CC6.7).
visual_for_abstractions: Each abstract sub-concept is a concrete DOM visual (ARIA, keyboard, no canvas): (1) a NAME is a chain of length-prefixed labels -> selecting 0x07 lights the next 7 bytes as one label and 0x00 glows as the end sentinel; (2) RECURSION DESIRED is a single bit -> the flags word 0x0100 expands to show RD as one lit bit; (3) RECURSIVE vs ITERATIVE -> stub->resolver as one round-trip, resolver->hierarchy as a descending referral staircase; (4) THE ENCRYPTION BOUNDARY -> a draggable divider that flips every stage card above it red 'in the clear' and below it green 'encrypted'; (5) ENFORCEMENT STRENGTH -> SPF ~all / DMARC p=reject as a policy dial none->quarantine->reject; (6) CERTIFICATE-ISSUANCE CONTROL -> CAA issue pki.goog draws one arrow domain->CA; (7) NAME==IDENTITY -> a drawn line links the cert SAN to the lifecycle SNI.

activities.name: PEEL the DNS query — read the bytes that carry the question
activities.mechanic: A real 29-byte DNS query for 'example.com A' rendered as a horizontal byte-ribbon (each octet a selectable DOM cell) above a collapsed RFC 1035 tree: Header (12 octets) / Question (17 octets). A ported RFC 1035 parser computes the true structure from the real bytes; every selectable region is generated from the parse tree. Selecting 0x07 lights the next 7 bytes ('example') as one label; the 0x00 terminator glows red. The flags word 0x0100 expands to show QR=0, Opcode=0, RD=1.
activities.sim_state: The real 29-byte query: 12 34 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65 03 63 6f 6d 00 00 01 00 01 — loaded as raw bytes; the ported RFC 1035 parser produces the region tree.

tasks.instruction: Select the 12-octet header. Then select the byte that contains QDCOUNT — confirm it reads as one question pending.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (selected range maps to parser's QDCOUNT region, bytes 10-11 = 0x00 0x01); field_value_is (QDCOUNT=1).
hint_ladder: The header is a fixed size in every DNS message — count octets from byte 0.
§ DNS message format — header packs ID, a flags word, then four 16-bit counts.
QDCOUNT is octets 10-11 (zero-indexed), value 0x0001.

tasks.instruction: Select the QNAME. Identify every length-prefix octet and the zero terminator, then decode the name the labels spell.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (QNAME region offset 12 through 0x00 at offset 24); decoded_artifact_matches (decoded name == parser's 'example.com').
hint_ladder: A name is not stored with dots — each chunk is preceded by a length byte.
§ Label encoding — 0x07 means 'next 7 bytes are a label'; 0x00 ends the name.
07 'example' 03 'com' 00 decodes to example.com.

tasks.instruction: Select the QTYPE and QCLASS fields and report what this query asks for.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (QTYPE [25,27), QCLASS [27,29)); field_value_is (QTYPE=1 A, QCLASS=1 IN).
hint_ladder: The last four octets sit right after the name terminator.
§ Resource record types — A=1, NS=2, CNAME=5; CLASS IN=1.
QTYPE 0x0001 = A, QCLASS 0x0001 = IN.

activities.honesty_source: The 29-byte query is the byte-exact RFC 1035 §4.1 message verified live via printf|xxd (label hex 6578616d706c65 / 636f6d confirmed). Every region/value shown is the ported RFC 1035 parser over the real bytes — the dissector is the oracle.
activities.new_engine_work: Port a tested RFC 1035 DNS message parser to TS (flags-word bit-unpacking, label/QNAME decoder, RR walker) as the PEEL oracle. New primitives region_labeled_correctly, field_value_is, decoded_artifact_matches. Fidelity-check against dig +qr.

activities.name: PEEL the DNS response — read the answer and its control flags
activities.mechanic: A real live-captured DNS response (Google DoH JSON for example.com) as an expandable tree: the flags row (RD/RA/AD) as labeled toggles showing real state, then the Answer section with each A record as a card (name/TYPE/TTL/RDATA). The AD (Authenticated Data) flag is a lit shield icon; selecting it reveals 'a validating resolver verified DNSSEC signatures'; a paired bad capture shows the shield grey = unvalidated.
activities.sim_state: Live DoH capture: {Status:0, RD:true, RA:true, AD:true, Answer:[{name:'example.com.',type:1,TTL:300,data:'104.20.23.154'},{name:'example.com.',type:1,TTL:300,data:'172.66.147.243'}]}.

tasks.instruction: Peel the Answer section. Report how many A records resolved and the RDATA (IP) of each.
tasks.machine_verify: field_value_is (count=2 and RDATA 104.20.23.154, 172.66.147.243 == parser decode).
hint_ladder: The Answer section is a list — each entry is one resource record.
§ RR format — NAME, TYPE, TTL, RDATA; an A record's RDATA is a 4-octet IPv4 address.

tasks.instruction: Peel the AD flag. State whether this answer was DNSSEC-validated, and name the one thing AD does NOT tell you about the query.
tasks.machine_verify: field_value_is (AD=true == parser flag); region_labeled_correctly (AD toggle maps to parsed AD bit).
hint_ladder: AD = Authenticated Data — set by the resolver, not the authoritative server.
§ DNSSEC vs DoH — DNSSEC authenticates the DATA; it does NOT encrypt the query.
AD=true means signatures were verified; it says nothing about whether the query travelled encrypted.

activities.honesty_source: Captured live via Google DoH JSON during research: Status:0, AD:true, two real A records TTL=300. Flag states and RR values are the parser's decode of the real captured JSON.
activities.new_engine_work: Reuse PEEL parser/oracle (extended to the DoH JSON shape: flags + Answer/Authority/Additional). Reuses region_labeled_correctly, field_value_is.

activities.name: TRACE the resolution treasure-hunt — recursive vs iterative
activities.mechanic: Participant nodes as a vertical hierarchy: Stub -> Recursive resolver -> Root NS -> .com TLD NS -> Authoritative NS. Real message cards (real query/referral content) dragged into the correct ordered sequence. Honest consequence: asking the root server directly for the final A record returns the REAL referral (root refers to .com, does not answer). The stub->recursive hop is drawn as ONE round-trip 'do all the work (RD=1)'; recursive->hierarchy as a descending staircase of referrals.
activities.sim_state: Live-captured chain: .com TLD nameservers (m/j/g/k.gtld-servers.net, TTL 21594); root NS list (a/b/c/j.root-servers.net); example.com authoritative answer (the two A records). The sim follows the real referral state machine.

tasks.instruction: Order the cards so the stub asks ONE recursive query and the recursive resolver walks root -> TLD -> authoritative iteratively. Route each message between the right nodes.
tasks.machine_verify: sequence_matches (stub->recursive RD=1; recursive->root; root referral->.com; recursive->.com TLD; TLD referral->authoritative; recursive->authoritative; authoritative answer); participant_routing_correct + sim accepts the full chain.
hint_ladder: Only ONE participant does all the legwork; everyone else points one step further.
§ Recursive vs iterative — the stub asks recursively; the resolver queries the hierarchy iteratively.
Stub->recursive (RD=1), then recursive->root (referral to .com), recursive->.com (referral to authoritative), recursive->authoritative (the A records), recursive->stub.

tasks.instruction: Route the final 'give me the A record for example.com' query directly to a root server. Read what the root returns and explain why the hunt can't be skipped.
tasks.machine_verify: participant_routing_correct (sim returns the REAL root referral — delegation to .com NS, no answer — and latches only when the learner records that the root referred).
hint_ladder: The root servers know one thing: who runs each TLD.
§ Delegation — each level is authoritative only for who runs the level below.
The root returns a referral to the .com TLD servers, never the A record.

activities.honesty_source: .com TLD nameservers (TTL 21594) and root server names captured live via DoH + dig . NS; canonical root list at iana.org/domains/root/servers. The sim's referral behaviour follows the real DNS delegation state machine.
activities.new_engine_work: TRACE surface with a stateful DNS-resolution sim following the real referral state machine. Reuses sequence_matches, participant_routing_correct.

activities.name: TRACE the full lifecycle + the encryption boundary
activities.mechanic: The integrative spine. Participants: Browser, Recursive resolver, Server (TCP/443). Message-stage cards — DNS query/response, TCP SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK, TLS ClientHello/ServerHello/(encrypted Finished), HTTP GET/200 — assembled into the chain that turns 'type google.com' into pixels. A draggable ENCRYPTION-BOUNDARY divider placed at the exact point confidentiality begins. Honest consequence: an HTTP GET before TLS Finished returns the REAL unexpected_message alert; the TCP ack number is checked (must equal peer seq+1). Each card is colour-coded clear (red) vs encrypted (green) relative to the boundary.
activities.sim_state: Real stage sequence: DNS (example.com A) -> TCP 3-way (ack=seq+1, RFC 9293) -> TLS 1.3 ClientHello(SNI+ALPN)->ServerHello->[encrypted] per RFC 8446 -> HTTP GET/200 per RFC 9110. Sim enforces RFC 8446 message order and the ack=seq+1 invariant.

tasks.instruction: Order every stage card from 'type google.com' to the rendered 200 OK, routing each between Browser, Resolver, and Server.
tasks.machine_verify: sequence_matches (DNS -> TCP(SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) -> TLS(ClientHello/ServerHello/Finished) -> HTTP(GET/200)); participant_routing_correct (DNS to resolver, rest to server); sim accepts the full chain.
hint_ladder: You can't open a connection to an address you don't have; you can't encrypt on a connection that isn't open.
§ The chain of trust — name resolves (DNS), transport opens (TCP), channel secured (TLS), app conversation runs (HTTP).
DNS first, then TCP SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK, then TLS ClientHello/ServerHello/Finished, then GET / and 200.

tasks.instruction: Drop the ENCRYPTION-BOUNDARY divider at the exact stage confidentiality begins. Then list every stage in the clear, including which TLS handshake fields leak.
tasks.machine_verify: region_labeled_correctly (boundary lands immediately after ServerHello); field_value_is (learner names DNS query, TCP handshake, ClientHello SNI/ALPN as plaintext == sim's cleartext set).
hint_ladder: Encryption can't exist before both sides have keys.
§ Where TLS begins — DNS lookup and TCP SYN are in the clear; SNI and ALPN ride in the plaintext ClientHello.
Boundary right after ServerHello; DNS, TCP, ClientHello SNI all travel unencrypted — DoH/DoT and ECH are mitigations.

tasks.instruction: Set the acknowledgment numbers on the SYN-ACK and ACK cards so the handshake completes.
tasks.machine_verify: sequence_matches / field_value_is (SYN-ACK ack == client ISN+1, final ACK ack == server ISN+1; sim completes only when both equal peer-seq+1).
hint_ladder: An acknowledgment says 'I received up through byte N, send me N next.'
§ TCP 3-way handshake — ack always equals peer sequence + 1.
SYN-ACK acks X with ack=X+1; the client's ACK acks Y with ack=Y+1.

activities.honesty_source: TCP invariant per RFC 9293; TLS 1.3 order + SNI/ALPN-in-ClientHello + post-ServerHello-encrypted per RFC 8446 §4.1 (reproducible via openssl s_client); HTTP per RFC 9110/9112; DNS stages reuse the live-captured example.com data.
